title: A minimal-width element of the kernel has invertible end coefficients and central terms, and division by it gives a finite free normal form

Elements of `T` are finite sums `h = Σ_k h_k x^k`, with `h_k in A`, and `x b = σ(b) x`. If `h != 0`, its
*width* is `max{k : h_k != 0} - min{k : h_k != 0}`. Since `x^-1` is a unit, `π` is onto: `R` is generated by `A` and
`x^±1`.

**Item 1.** Suppose `J != 0`, and let `m` be the least width of a nonzero element of `J`.
- **Normalizing.** Left multiplication by a power of `x` moves the support of an element of `J` to start at `0`.
  Let `I_0` be the set of `c in A` such that some `g in J` has support in `[0, m]` and `g_0 = c`.
  - `I_0` is an ideal: `(b g)_0 = b g_0` and `(g b)_0 = g_0 b`.
  - It is `σ`-invariant: `x g x^-1 = Σ σ(g_k) x^k` and `x^-1 g x = Σ σ^-1(g_k) x^k` have the same support.
  - It is nonzero, so `I_0 = A`, and some `g in J` has support in `[0, m]` and `g_0 = 1`.
  - Minimality forces `g_m != 0`. If `m = 0`, then `1 in J` and `R = 0`. So `m >= 1`.
- **Commutation.**
  - For `b in A`, `b g - g b in J` has `0`-th coefficient `b - b = 0` and support in `[1, m]`, so width at most
    `m - 1`. Hence it is `0`, which gives `b g_k = g_k σ^k(b)`.
  - Likewise `x g x^-1 - g = 0`, which gives `σ(g_k) = g_k`.
  - So each `g_k x^k` commutes with `A` and with `x`, and is central in `T`.
- **The top coefficient is a unit.**
  - `b g_m = g_m σ^m(b)` gives `A g_m = g_m A`, a two-sided ideal. It is `σ`-invariant because `σ(g_m) = g_m`, and
    nonzero, so it is `A`.
  - So `c g_m = 1` and `g_m d = 1` for some `c, d`, and `g_m` is a unit. Then `σ^m(b) = g_m^-1 b g_m`.
- **`J = T g`.** `g` is central, so `T g = g T` is an ideal inside `J`.
  - **Division.** Let `h in T` have top degree `n >= m` with top coefficient `h_n`. Subtracting `c x^(n-m) g`, with
    `c = h_n σ^(n-m)(g_m)^-1`, lowers the top degree. Let `h` have bottom degree `e < 0` with bottom coefficient
    `h_e`. Subtracting `h_e x^e g` raises the bottom degree, since `g_0 = 1`. So every `h` is congruent modulo `T g`
    to an element with support in `[0, m-1]`.
  - **Uniqueness.** An element of `J` with support in `[0, m-1]` has width less than `m`, so it is `0`. So each
    `h in J` reduces to `0`, and `J = T g`.

**Item 2.** If `J = 0`, then `R = T` is graded by the power of `x`, with `x in R_1` a unit. That is the hypothesis
of the graded node.

**Item 3.**
- **(a)** By the division and uniqueness steps, the classes of `x^k`, `0 <= k < m`, form a basis of `R = T / T g` as a
  left `A`-module. Since `A x^k = x^k A`, they are also a basis of it as a right module.
- **(b)** Let `A''` be the subring generated by `S = ∪_(0 <= j < m) σ^j(F) ∪ {g_1, ..., g_m, g_m^-1}`.
  - `σ^(±1)(A'') ⊆ A''`. `σ` maps `σ^j(F)` to `σ^(j+1)(F)`, and `σ^m(F) = g_m^-1 F g_m`. `σ^-1(F) = σ^(m-1)(σ^-m(F))`, and
    this equals `g_m σ^(m-1)(F) g_m^-1`, using `σ(g_m) = g_m`. The `g_k` are fixed.
  - So the elements `Σ c_k x^k`, with `c_k in A''`, form a subring of `R` containing `F` and `x^±1`. That subring is
    all of `R`.
  - Dividing by `g`, whose coefficients and the inverse `g_m^-1` lie in `A''`, puts every element of `R` in the form
    `Σ_(k < m) c_k x^k` with `c_k in A''`.
  - For `a in A`, the normal form `a = a x^0` is unique by (a), so `a in A''`.
- **(c)** Inner automorphisms act trivially on `K_n`, and `σ^m = Ad(g_m^-1)`.
- **(d)**
  - `R` is a finitely generated free `A`-module, so restriction of scalars sends finitely generated projective
    `R`-modules to finitely generated projective `A`-modules. `R_A ≅ A^m` gives `[1_R] -> m[1_A]`.
  - `R ⊗_A P = ⊕_(k < m) x^k A ⊗_A P`. With `x a = σ(a) x`, `x^k A` is `A` with its left action twisted by `σ^(-k)`, so its
    class is `σ^(-k)_*[P]`. The sum over `0 <= k < m` is the same either way, since `σ^m_* = 1` (gq-referee-a, N2).
  - **`Q ⊆ A`.** For an integer `n >= 1`, multiplication by `n` is bijective on `R = ⊕ A x^k`, so it is bijective on
    `A`, and `1 = n c` for some `c in A`.
  - `Q^x -> K_1(R)` factors through `K_1(A)`, which gives the kernel inclusion.

**Item 4.**
- Restriction is a homomorphism, so `[1_R] = n c` gives `m[1_A] = n · res(c)`: `m[1_A]` is divisible by every `n`.
- Induction sends `[1_A]` to `[1_R]`, so `ind(m[1_A]) = m[1_R]`. If `t m[1_A] = 0` for some `t >= 1`, then
  `t m [1_R] = 0`. So `m[1_A]` has infinite order when `[1_R]` does.
- A subgroup of a finitely generated abelian group is finitely generated. So `K_1` detection passes to `A` by (d).
- By (c), `σ_*` has finite order on `K_0(A)`. So the orbit of a class under the symmetry is finite.
